summary: Sirach 38 first tells the student to honor physicians, medicines, prayer, repentance, and offerings as parts of seeking healing. It then turns to death, urging real lament but warning against being consumed by sorrow. The chapter closes by contrasting the leisure needed for scribal wisdom with the indispensable labor of farmers, artisans, smiths, and potters who sustain city life.
whyItMatters: This chapter shows Sirach joining reverence for God to ordinary embodied life: sickness, medical skill, grief, work, and learning. It also exposes a social tension in the book: manual workers are honored as necessary, yet scribal wisdom is still treated as a distinct vocation requiring leisure.

context.author: Yeshua son of Eleazar son of Sira, a Jerusalem teacher and scribe; his unnamed grandson later translated the Hebrew work into Greek in Egypt.
context.audience: Students seeking disciplined wisdom in Jerusalem, and later Greek-reading Jewish audiences who received the grandson's translation.
context.date: The Hebrew work was composed in the early second century BC and was likely complete around 180–175 BC. The grandson arrived in Egypt around 132 BC and translated it during his stay.
context.setting: Jerusalem under Hellenistic rule, with temple worship, scribal education, ordinary trades, and Greek-speaking Mediterranean pressures in the background.
context.literaryForm: Wisdom instruction: poetic teaching and practical maxims that form judgment in worship, household life, society, work, sickness, grief, and death.

outline.heading: Honor the physician and medicines
outline.note: Healing, medical skill, medicines from the earth, and the pharmacist's work are presented as gifts within God's created order.

outline.heading: Seek God and accept medical help
outline.note: In sickness the student is told to pray, turn from wrongdoing, make offerings, and give place to the physician, whose work also depends on prayer.

outline.heading: Grieve the dead with limits
outline.note: The chapter commands tears, lamentation, burial, and remembrance, while warning that unbounded sorrow harms the living.

outline.heading: The leisure of the scribe
outline.note: Scribal wisdom is said to require opportunity and freedom from constant business.

outline.heading: The labor of farmers and artisans
outline.note: Plowman, craftsman, smith, and potter are absorbed in their work. Ben Sira excludes them from public judgment and teaching roles while calling their skilled labor indispensable to the city.

keyVerses.text: The Lord created medicines out of the earth. A prudent man will not despise them.
keyVerses.why: This verse anchors the chapter's unusually direct affirmation of medicines as part of created provision.

keyVerses.text: My son, in your sickness don’t be negligent, but pray to the Lord, and he will heal you.
keyVerses.why: This begins the direct instruction to the student about illness, joining practical care with prayer.

keyVerses.text: My son, let your tears fall over the dead, and as one who suffers grievously, begin lamentation. Wind up his body with due honor. Don’t neglect his burial.
keyVerses.why: This verse opens the chapter's teaching on grief, requiring public care for the dead rather than emotional avoidance.

keyVerses.text: But they will maintain the fabric of the age. Their prayer is in the handiwork of their craft.
keyVerses.why: The closing verse gives dignity to the workers just described, even after noting their distance from scribal offices.

questions.question: Does this chapter approve of using physicians and medicines?
questions.answer: Yes. The chapter tells the reader to honor a physician, says the Lord created him, and says medicines were created out of the earth. It does not set prayer and medical care against each other; the student is told to pray and then to give place to the physician.

questions.question: What does the chapter mean by “physician”?
questions.answer: In this chapter the physician is a skilled healer who should be honored according to need. The text says the physician's skill brings public esteem and that recovery can at times be in such hands. It also says physicians ask the Lord to prosper them in diagnosis and healing.

questions.question: Why are prayer, repentance, offerings, and the physician all mentioned together?
questions.answer: The chapter treats sickness as a moment for whole-person response. The student is told not to be negligent, to pray, to put away wrongdoing, to make an offering according to means, and then to make room for the physician. The text does not explain every illness as punishment; it gives a pattern of religious and practical response.

questions.question: What should a reader do with verse 15, where the sinner falls into the hands of the physician?
questions.answer: Verse 15 sounds like a judgment on someone who sins before his Maker: he is to fall into the physician’s hands. It does not explain whether the treatment itself is expected to be a hardship. The surrounding verses honor physicians as created by the Lord and describe their prayer for successful healing, so this severe saying has to be read alongside that praise.

questions.question: Does Sirach tell people not to grieve?
questions.answer: No. The chapter commands tears, lamentation, honoring the body, and burial. Verse 17 specifies one or two days of wailing and links that observance to public reputation; the following lines urge comfort and warn against sorrow that harms the living. This reflects Ben Sira’s ancient expectations for mourning, rather than establishing a timetable for every person’s grief.

questions.question: Why does the chapter say, “yesterday for him, and today for you”?
questions.answer: The line uses another person’s death to remind the living of their own mortality. It comes after instructions to mourn and bury the dead with honor. Ben Sira appeals to the common human future to urge the mourner toward comfort, while also insisting that grief cannot bring the dead person back.

questions.question: Why does the chapter say the scribe needs leisure?
questions.answer: Verse 24 says the wisdom of the scribe comes by the opportunity of leisure, and that someone with little business can become wise. The next verses contrast this with workers whose tasks absorb their attention day and night. The chapter presents scribal wisdom as a demanding vocation that requires time for study and judgment.

questions.question: Is the chapter looking down on manual workers?
questions.answer: The chapter gives a mixed picture. It says farmers and artisans are not sought in council, do not sit as judges, and do not declare instruction and judgment. Yet it also says they are skillful, that no city would be inhabited without them, and that they maintain the fabric of the age. Readers should notice both the hierarchy of scribal learning and the real honor given to necessary craft.

questions.question: What is meant by “Their prayer is in the handiwork of their craft”?
questions.answer: The line links the workers' devotion to the work of their hands. It does not say they replace prayer with labor; earlier the chapter speaks plainly of praying to the Lord. Here the closing thought dignifies faithful craft as the sphere where these workers express their calling.

glossary.def: A healer whose skill is to be honored and whose help the sick person should not dismiss.
Remedies described as created out of the earth and not to be despised by a prudent person.
A maker of mixtures used in healing, named alongside medicines and God's works.
Public grieving over the dead, paired here with tears, wailing, burial, and eventual comfort.
A learned teacher or writer whose wisdom, in this chapter, depends on leisure and freedom from constant business.
The smith's work surface, used here as part of a vivid picture of difficult, skilled metalwork.
